1. The Proposition and Where It Lands

Proposition: can Go's goroutine be brought into SA? The discussion converged on this landing place: it does not enter the SA specification — the SA base is frozen (registers + the ownership/capability specification stay stable and do not yield to any single frontend); a goroutine is essentially a runtime capability and should land in the sa_std runtime core, with the upper syntax surfaces (SLA's spawn surface, go2sa's go statement) being mere surface sugar. In positioning it belongs to the foundational core, fitting the architecture doctrine that “all foundational cores are built into sa_std, and plugins only do the wrapping/framework layer”: without it, every upper-layer consumer of goroutine semantics would have to build its own scheduler wheel.

2. Why SA Suits goroutines Even Better

  • No GC entanglement: the hardest half of Go's scheduler is its cooperation with the GC — stack scanning for roots and per-pointer fixups when stacks are copied. SA is an ownership model with no GC, so that half of the cost simply does not exist: stacks need no GC scanning, and with no stack copying in v1 there is no pointer-fixup problem either.
  • Channels can statically prevent races: a channel carrying ownership values can be statically verified by the checker with Send-like semantics (sending hands over, receiving acquires), forming the combination “goroutines without a GC + channels that prevent data races at compile time” — something Go itself cannot offer, and the core highlight that distinguishes this proposition from “yet another coroutine library”.
  • Two foundation pieces are already in place: F-perf-1's sa_std_net_poll_wait is the counterpart of Go's netpoller (already landed, already adopted by slaredis); std's pthread surface is also present. The only gap is the middle layer: context switching + an M:N scheduler.

3. The v1 Shape (discussion draft; scope follows the ruling)

  • Stackful coroutines, not stackless (stackless cannot suspend deep inside arbitrary functions, which does not match goroutine semantics).
  • Each goroutine has a fixed virtual stack reservation + guard pages committed on demand, and stack overflow traps explicitly; phase one does not do Go-style copying stack growth, and the cap is written out, not silent.
  • Context switching is done for x86_64 first (on the order of a hundred lines of assembly per architecture); whether the other architectures are in the same batch is S5.
  • The scheduler is written in Zig in sa_std: a run queue + work stealing + park/unpark; all network I/O goes through the netpoller (sa_std_net_poll_wait) and does not block carrier threads.
  • Preemption in phase one is cooperative: the frontend inserts yield points at call sites, loop back-edges, and channel operations (the same as Go before 1.14); signal-based asynchronous preemption is left to phase two — whether phase one does it is S2.
  • A blocking file syscall will block a carrier thread: either the scheduler's thread pool compensates, or phase one explicitly guarantees only non-blocking network I/O, with files going through thread offloading — either treatment must be explicitly registered; no silent fallback is allowed.

4. Hard Boundaries

  • The wasm target: in principle goroutines can be supported (user correction, 2026-10-29: Go's official wasm port is itself the proof; feasible paths include Asyncify-style binary transformation, compiler-level stack-state transformation, the Wasm stack-switching proposal / JSPI, and so on), but it cannot be implemented with phase one's x86_64 native stack-pointer switching mechanism and must take an independent lowering track. So phase one still states UNSUPPORTED for wasm, with the registration's nature being a mechanism difference, not a denial in principle, written into the contract.
  • goroutine ≠ GC: bringing in goroutines does not solve go2sa's heap-object memory story; that is an independent unsolved item and the two must not be conflated.
  • Calling a blocking extern (FFI) inside a goroutine will block a carrier thread; this constraint must enter the runtime contract documentation, at the caller's own responsibility.

5. Downstream Value

This runtime does not only pave the way for go2sa's go statement: slanginx's per-connection model, slaredis's connection handling, and db's service-ization candidates all eat the same M:N runtime. After the networking core, it is sa_std's second foundational-core candidate of the kind “without it, the upper layer has to build its own wheel”.

6. Scope Awaiting a Jev Ruling

The following six items are open questions, worded exactly as the ruling questions; the ruling results decide the phase-one scope and the later phasing, and this page does not prejudge them:

  • S1 Stack model: a fixed virtual stack reservation per goroutine + an explicit trap on overflow, or copying stack growth already in phase one?
  • S2 Preemption: cooperative in phase one (the frontend inserts yield points at call sites, loop back-edges, and channel operations), or signal-based asynchronous preemption already in phase one?
  • S3 Surface scope: do the built-in SLA syntax surface and go2sa land in the same batch, or does go2sa go first in phase one with the SLA surface postponed?
  • S4 Channel semantics scope: full delivery of unbuffered + buffered + select in phase one, or only the unbuffered minimal set?
  • S5 Architecture scope: x86_64 only in phase one, or x86_64 and aarch64 in the same batch?
  • S6 sync primitives: are synchronization primitives such as Mutex / WaitGroup delivered in the same batch as phase one?

7. Jev Ruling (2026-10-29)

Ruling (2026-10-29, jev-1.14.0, item-by-item two-option noul comparisons, ruling file ~/workspace/jev-designs/goroutine_scope_ruling.json):

  • S1 Stack model: selected a fixed virtual stack reservation + guard pages committed on demand + an explicit trap on overflow (0.81); copying stack growth not selected (0.09).
  • S2 Preemption: selected cooperative in phase one (the frontend inserts yield points at call sites / loop back-edges / channel operations) (0.75); signal-based asynchronous preemption not selected (0.17).
  • S3 Surface scope: selected go2sa first, the built-in SLA syntax surface postponed (0.61); both surfaces in the same batch not selected (0.43). The sa_std runtime extern surface is unchanged; what is postponed is only the SLA compiler's syntax/checker work.
  • S4 Channel semantics: selected unbuffered + buffered + select in full (0.49); the unbuffered-only minimal set not selected (0.30). This item's winning confidence is the lowest of the six; in implementation, select's multi-way wait registration is designed natively on the scheduler's park queue, not patched together after the fact.
  • S5 Architecture: selected x86_64 only in phase one (0.82); x86_64+aarch64 in the same batch not selected (0.17).
  • S6 sync primitives: selected delivered in the same batch as phase one (Mutex/RwLock/WaitGroup/Once, built on the park queue) (0.69); not including them in phase one not selected (0.57).

Phase-one scope convergence: a fixed-stack cooperative M:N scheduling runtime (sa_std, x86_64) + full channels/select + sync primitives, with the surface serving go2sa first and the built-in SLA surface in phase two.

8. SLA Syntax Surface and Ecosystem Uplift Discussion, and the S3 Re-Ruling (2026-10-29)

Discussion proposition (the user): if goroutines really are brought in, SLA must also add the corresponding syntax — how much does that lift the whole ecosystem? The main-session evaluation converged: the lift is mainly at the application layer, and it is structural.

  • Server forms return to their proper shape: the three servers slanginx / slaredis / db no longer hand-build their own concurrency models — slaredis's single-threaded poll loop + sharded wait sets, slanginx's F2 concurrent serve, which to this day has no native answer, and db's concurrency, trapped in the Zig-layer epoch model where SLA cannot reach it; with go + channel + select, all of them can be written as “one piece of sequential code per connection”.
  • Eliminating function coloring: SLA's existing async is stackless, with the async/sync worlds sharply divided; stackful goroutines let any function block, so everyday concurrent code no longer needs to be colored for asynchrony.
  • Nativizing the CXU backend seams: concurrent-shaped seams such as bridging pumps, long polling, child-process management, and streaming forwarding are currently stitched together with callbacks and polling; goroutines + select are their native shape.
  • Ecosystem positioning: once the SLA syntax surface lands, the ecosystem positioning converges to “Go's concurrency model + ownership checking + no GC”; an extern surface alone cannot support that positioning.

What it does not lift: single-threaded performance numbers (the 99% target is fought on std implementation quality, and scheduling overhead is even slightly higher than a hand-tuned event loop) and the compiler's existing defect stock — not one of them is solved by this. The cost: the checker must add channel-payload ownership rules and spawn capture rules (what a goroutine may capture, and whether by move or by borrow — Go does not care, but we cannot not care), plus the interoperability stance with the existing stackless async; all of this is real design work.

Premise change: the original Section 7 S3 ruling (go2sa first 0.61 / both surfaces in one batch 0.43) rested on go2sa consuming the runtime first; the user has now set go2sa / cpp2sa aside with no resumption date, SLA becomes the runtime's only consumption surface, and calling externs directly is only an acceptance form, not an ecosystem form — the ordering rationale no longer exists, hence the re-ruling.

Jev re-ruling (2026-10-29, jev-1.14.0, ruling file ~/workspace/jev-designs/goroutine_s3_reruling.json):

  • The premise has substantively changed: 0.89.
  • New ordering: the SLA syntax surface immediately follows the runtime phase-one acceptance (0.83) — the batch includes the go/spawn statement, the channel type, the select statement, checker rules for channel-payload ownership and spawn capture, and the interoperability stance with the existing async; checker design may overlap runtime Period C, but SLA compiler code must not land before the runtime acceptance.
  • Not selected: keeping the original S3 posture and waiting for the go2sa era (0.51); starting immediately in parallel with the runtime (0.14).

Accordingly, the convergence sentence in Section 7, “the surface serves go2sa first, the built-in SLA surface in phase two”, is changed from this section on to: immediately after the runtime phase-one acceptance comes the SLA syntax-surface batch, and when go2sa is re-proposed as a project it directly inherits the already-verified surface.

11. Runtime Contract in Writing (1): The Yield-Point Set and the select Selection Strategy (2026-10-29)

The yield-point set (TS-13): phase-one preemption is cooperative (see Section 3), and its yield-point set is now enumerated in writing — a yield point = an explicit sa_task_yield extern call site + every blocking runtime call. The SLA compiler inserts no yields at all: no loop back-edge yields, no call-site yields. The blocking runtime call set (enumerated per the implementation): chan send / recv / select, sa_task_join, sa_task_sleep_ns / sa_task_sleep_ms, sa_task_net_wait, and the parking path of sa_sync_mutex_lock. A compute-dense goroutine that calls none of the above entry points will starve a carrier thread; this is stated behavior, self-evident from the runtime's header comments, not a defect.

The select selection strategy (Register No. 2): the readiness selection of sa_chan_select has two phases. Phase 1 (immediate evaluation): try each case in declaration order by case index, and the first ready one returns immediately — the immediate phase has a declaration-order bias; Phase 2 (after parking): the first arriving peer claims it via selectTryClaim — first come, first served in time order. The overall stance is not Go-style uniform pseudo-random selection, and code that depends on selection fairness must be written to this stance. select's timeout timing uses a monotonic clock (for the stance, see the “Clock stance” section of the stdlib time page).

timeout(0) polling semantics (supplementary note, 2026-11-01): after the runtime select fast path landed (sci main 531af60d: the ready phase is judged first, and when nothing is ready and the timeout is 0, no waiter is registered to park), a select with timeout(0) and no ready arm returns not-ready immediately and no longer parks — the roughly 100µs pseudo-yield that its former park/wake round trip carried has been eliminated. A pure timeout(0) polling loop therefore becomes a true busy spin (consistent with Go); code that needs to yield must explicitly yield or use a positive timeout, and must not rely on timeout(0)'s old incidental yield.

The positioning of R2 (TS-14): the checker's only effect-class product is the is_async boolean on a function signature; the signature table has no blocking / effect field. Effect rule R2 is a shallow syntactic rule with only two checkpoints — Chan send / recv method calls appearing directly in an async function body, and a select with no default / timeout fallback — gated by a single traversal state that resets on entering a closure body. Its coverage ends there: it does not reach transitive calls (blocking inside a synchronous fn leaves no mark, and an async fn calling it does not trigger R2), and it does not reach direct extern calls (blocking externs such as sa_task_sleep_ns, sa_chan_*, and sa_sync_mutex_lock are checked as ordinary calls). There currently does not exist any product such as a transitive blockable set, a blocking-extern list, or a call-graph appendix — occasions that need a blockability conclusion (asynchronous coloring for stackless targets, native-side blocking audits) must compute it themselves, with no official appendix to rely on. If a transitive coloring appendix is added, it is a new checker analysis pass, scheduled separately; this paragraph only puts the positioning in writing.

12. Memory Model: The Contract for Synchronization Edges (TS-15, 2026-10-29)

SA previously had no written memory model; the following six surfaces are written as a contract following the synchronization discipline of the current runtime implementation (implementation sources: sci src/runtime/sa_task.zig, src/runtime/sa_globals.zig, and the LLVM emission layer). This section is the correctness foundation for Ordering Two (the three machines' goroutine rework); all six surfaces rest on the current implementation, and if the implementation changes, this section must be revised with it.

  • chan: payload movement is completed entirely inside the channel's futex mutex (the lock is implemented as a cmpxchg .acquire / swap .release + futex wait/wake); a send writes the buffer or delivers directly to a receiver inside the lock, and a receive takes it away inside the lock. This forms a synchronization edge in the implementation: one send synchronizes-before the completion of its paired recv.
  • select: claiming is completed inside the select mutex (sel.mu); the payload is written by the claimant into the waiting node's slot inside the channel lock, and only then is the select owner woken (unpark); the waiting node's reference count (SelectWaiter.refs) uses .seq_cst.
  • spawn / join: goroutine exit converges on a single convergence point (goroutineExit); the trap record is written final before join waiters are woken. Reading trap information after join returns is therefore safe in the implementation.
  • User Mutex (sa_sync_mutex_*): a goroutine-aware parking lock whose underlying synchronization follows the same futex Mutex acquire / release pairing as channels; it is non-reentrant — re-entry returns ERR_INVALID (as the implementation comments state).
  • globals: all get / set / add operations are serialized by a single global mutex, so globals operations are totally ordered serially and naturally form happens-before edges; add is a wrapping read-modify-write (RMW).
  • SA atomic instructions: instructions carry an ordering field; LLVM emission defaults to .seq_cst when nothing else is specified.

13. Runtime Contract in Writing (2): Stack Shape and Recursion Depth (TS-18, 2026-10-29)

Recursion depth takes three forms, with three overflow treatments, on three execution surfaces; this section writes them down per the current state of the implementation (including one undefined case, written as it is):

  • Goroutines: fully defined. A fixed virtual stack, with usable space of 256 KiB by default (adjustable via the env SA_TASK_STACK_KIB), with guard pages; on overflow, the runtime's SIGSEGV handler recognizes the guard page address, prints sa_task: goroutine <id> stack overflow, and aborts — loud, but the stack is already lost and it cannot be recovered at the goroutine boundary.
  • The interpreter path: a written value. The call-depth cap is 1024 frames; exceeding it returns RunError.CallStackOverflow, mapped to exit code 108 — a clean error rather than a crash; the guard triggers before the host stack grows.
  • The compiled path's main line (main and ordinary call chains): currently undefined. main is not a goroutine — the C entry wrapper calls the program's main directly on the host process's main thread, and SA function frames run on the host OS thread stack throughout; the implementation sets no main-thread stack size anywhere, so the cap is the host main-thread stack (the Linux default rlimit, typically 8 MiB) divided by the frame size — no language-level value, floating with frame size, not portable. Overflow is a SIGSEGV with no “recursion too deep” diagnostic at all: when the task runtime is initialized, the handler confirms the fault address is not a guard page, then restores the default signal handling and dies by the original signal; when uninitialized, it is a bare SIGSEGV. The compiled path's @test main line gets the same treatment (only goroutines spawned inside a test take the 256 KiB defined stack).

That is: for the same deeply recursive program, the interpreter path gives a deterministic error at 1024 frames, a goroutine gives a loud trap with an id, and the compiled path's main line gives a SIGSEGV with no diagnostic — the inconsistency of the three surfaces is the current state. Defining the compiled main line's stack depth (making the entry thread stack explicit, or depth counting) is a code-surface candidate (a batch-three candidate, to be ruled only after empirical probing on the box in the same batch); this section only puts the current state in writing.

Related discussion: cpp2sa and go2sa: Proposal Discussion for Two New Frontends (go2sa's goroutine/channel semantics follow this page's runtime ruling).

The recovery line's measured gates: the sci gate = sa-std-static (RC=0) + nm sa_task_* (T symbols) exactly 15 + sa-std-unit's failure set in two rounds exactly {keyring} (round 1: 313/314, failure name set exactly {keyring}; round 2: 313/314, failure name set exactly {keyring} — the total of 314 = the old 313 + 1 new monitor regression, which passed in both rounds, and a previously observed unattributed first-round flake did not reproduce); the sla gate = the merged tree @6004af4 with .sla-cache cleared, the plugin rebuilt and reinstalled (RC=0, with the same round's md5 for built and installed both 93e74aa387b68b94fb6eab359cb1e135), and the corpus10 normalized-set comparison (34 entries × 〈rc, counts, sorted failure name set〉) giving a difference set of 0 and zero new failures (the baseline signature being two families of known base-point defects; the raw text diff of 3 lines = a name-ordering difference + 2 non-deterministic panic codes from the base-point defect families, not new failures).

15. Usage Examples (measured on the box on 2026-10-30)

The following seven examples were measured and passed on a Colab box on 2026-10-30 with the then-current master toolchain: sa 0.1.8, the sla plugin @6004af4, sci @e7c18568; the build command was SA_PLUGIN_DEV=1 sa sla build-exe <例>.sla (that 2026-10-30 snapshot emitted SAB at the time; since 2026-11-15 this command defaults to SA text emission, see the “Feature Maturity Matrix”), and the output below is the programs' real stdout (each example run at least 3 times in a row consistently, Example 3 run 10 times in a row). The forms are trimmed from the delivered acceptance corpus (the gosyntax acceptance set and the test_unit_go_* corpus), with only scale reductions and main + println presentation applied, and the syntax forms preserved verbatim. Stance note: calling sa build-exe <例>.sla directly by extension on the host currently takes the text emission surface, and the examples in this section that contain globals string keys will hit leftover (1) of Section 14 (set / get with the same key acting as different keys, reading back 0), so sa sla build-exe is uniformly authoritative; the two-step form (sa sla sab build producing a .sab, then sa build-exe on that .sab) was also measured equivalent (verified by Example 1).

Example 1 · go Launch and join

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/globals.sai"
@import "sa_std/task.sai"
fn bump(arg: u64) {
    let out: u64 = 0;
    let rc = sa_global_u64_add("acc_ctr", 8, 3, &out);
    if rc != 0 { panic(101); };
}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let rc0 = sa_global_u64_set("acc_ctr", 8, 0);
    if rc0 != 0 { panic(102); };
    let handles: [u64; 8] = [0; 8];
    let i: u64 = 0;
    while i < 8 {
        let h = go bump(0);
        handles[i] = h;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    let j: u64 = 0;
    while j < 8 {
        let st = sa_task_join(handles[j]);
        if st != 0 { panic(103); };
        j = j + 1;
    }
    let v: u64 = 0;
    let rc = sa_global_u64_get("acc_ctr", 8, &v);
    println("total = {}", v);
    return 0;
}

Measured output:

total = 24

Each of the 8 goroutines adds +3 to the shared atomic cell; after the handles are collected into an array, each is sa_task_joined in turn (a return of 0 = normal exit), for a total of 24 = 8 × 3.

Example 2 · Chan Request / Reply (ping-pong)

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/task.sai"
fn pp_worker(ch: Chan<u64>) {
    let (v1, closed1) = ch.recv();
    if closed1 { panic(201); };
    ch.send(v1 + 1);
    let (v2, closed2) = ch.recv();
    if closed2 { panic(202); };
    ch.send(v2 + 1);
}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let ch: Chan<u64> = Chan::new(0);
    let h = go pp_worker(ch);
    ch.send(10);
    let (r1, c1) = ch.recv();
    if c1 { panic(203); };
    println("reply = {}", r1);
    ch.send(20);
    let (r2, c2) = ch.recv();
    if c2 { panic(204); };
    println("reply = {}", r2);
    let st = sa_task_join(h);
    if st != 0 { panic(205); };
    ch.destroy();
    return 0;
}

Measured output:

reply = 11
reply = 21

The channel handle is passed to the goroutine by value (handles are copyable; payload ownership moves with send); on an unbuffered channel, send / recv rendezvous in pairs, and the worker replies +1 each round. Note: the form in which a Chan field is embedded in a struct and then materialized through a Box has a registered defect (leftover (2) of Section 14); this example uses the direct-handle-passing form.

Example 3 · select Multi-Way Collection

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/task.sai"
fn producer(ch: Chan<u64>) {
    let i: u64 = 0;
    while i < 10 {
        ch.send(1);
        i = i + 1;
    }
}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let a: Chan<u64> = Chan::new(16);
    let b: Chan<u64> = Chan::new(16);
    let h1 = go producer(a);
    let h2 = go producer(b);
    let total: u64 = 0;
    let got: u64 = 0;
    while got < 20 {
        select {
            case let (v, closed) = a.recv() {
                total = total + v;
                got = got + 1;
            }
            case let (v, closed) = b.recv() {
                total = total + v;
                got = got + 1;
            }
            timeout(10000000000) { panic(301); }
        }
    }
    let s1 = sa_task_join(h1);
    let s2 = sa_task_join(h2);
    println("collected = {}", total);
    a.destroy();
    b.destroy();
    return 0;
}

Measured output:

collected = 20

Each of the two producers sends ten 1s; select receives whenever one way is ready, the cross-channel arrival order is free, and the total is determined. The timeout arm is a 10-second fallback; a buffer of 16 keeps the producers from blocking.

Example 4 · defer's LIFO and Argument Snapshots

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/globals.sai"
fn log_digit(v: i64) {
    let cur: u64 = 0;
    let rc1 = sa_global_u64_get("acc_dlog", 8, &cur);
    if rc1 != 0 { panic(401); };
    let rc2 = sa_global_u64_set("acc_dlog", 8, cur * 10 + (v as u64));
    if rc2 != 0 { panic(402); };
}
fn defer_fn() -> i64 {
    defer log_digit(1);
    let x: i64 = 2;
    defer log_digit(x);
    x = 9;
    {
        defer log_digit(3);
        log_digit(4);
    }
    if x == 9 {
        defer log_digit(5);
        return 7;
    };
    return 0;
}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let rc0 = sa_global_u64_set("acc_dlog", 8, 0);
    let r = defer_fn();
    let cur: u64 = 0;
    let rc = sa_global_u64_get("acc_dlog", 8, &cur);
    println("order = {}", cur);
    return 0;
}

Measured output:

order = 43521

The output digit string, digit by digit, is the execution order: 4 (the statement executed directly) → 3 (the inner block exits) → 5 (the if block on the early-return path) → 2 (the snapshot of x at registration time, not the later-changed 9) → 1 (the outermost layer). defer is block-scoped and last-in, first-out.

Example 5 · supervised: trap → recover → Restart

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/globals.sai"
@import "sa_std/task.sai"
@import "sa_std/supervisor.sla"
fn flaky(arg: u64) {
    let n: u64 = 0;
    let rc = sa_global_u64_add("acc_attempts", 8, 1, &n);
    if rc != 0 { panic(501); };
    if n <= 2 {
        let ch: Chan<u64> = Chan::new(0);
        ch.close();
        ch.close();
    };
}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let r0 = sa_global_u64_set("acc_attempts", 8, 0);
    let notify: Chan<(u64, i32)> = Chan::new(8);
    let policy = supervise_policy(3, 60000);
    let result = supervise(flaky, 0, policy, notify);
    if result != 0 { panic(502); };
    let (m1, ok1) = notify.recv();
    println("exit 1 code = {}", m1.1);
    let (m2, ok2) = notify.recv();
    println("exit 2 code = {}", m2.1);
    let (m3, ok3) = notify.recv();
    println("exit 3 code = {}", m3.1);
    let attempts: u64 = 0;
    let rc = sa_global_u64_get("acc_attempts", 8, &attempts);
    println("attempts = {}", attempts);
    notify.destroy();
    return 0;
}

Measured output:

exit 1 code = 4
exit 2 code = 4
exit 3 code = 0
attempts = 3

flaky's first two runs trigger a goroutine boundary trap (code 4) with a double close; the std supervisor supervise reads back the trap record, delivers (handle, code) over the notify channel, and restarts within the restart budget, and the third run succeeds (code 0). Boundary recover is not a general exception system (see Section 3 of Document 15).

Example 6 · monitor: Exit Notification as a Message

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/task.sai"
fn mon_ok(arg: u64) {
    let rc = sa_task_yield();
    if rc != 0 { panic(601); };
}
fn mon_bad(arg: u64) {
    let ch: Chan<u64> = Chan::new(0);
    ch.close();
    ch.close();
}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let h1 = go mon_ok(0);
    let h2 = go supervised mon_bad(0);
    let m1 = monitor(h1);
    let m2 = monitor(h2);
    let got: u64 = 0;
    while got < 2 {
        select {
            case let (msg, closed) = m1.recv() {
                println("h1 exit code = {}", msg.1);
                got = got + 1;
            }
            case let (msg, closed) = m2.recv() {
                println("h2 exit code = {}", msg.1);
                got = got + 1;
            }
            timeout(10000000000) { panic(602); }
        }
    }
    let s1 = sa_task_join(h1);
    let s2 = sa_task_join(h2);
    m1.destroy();
    m2.destroy();
    return 0;
}

Measured output:

h1 exit code = 0
h2 exit code = 4

monitor(handle) returns a Chan<(u64, i32)>: a normal exit delivers code 0 and a supervised child's boundary trap delivers code 4, and both can continue to be received with select. The two notifications' arrival order follows scheduling; in this example's repeated measurements, h1 came first every time.

Example 7 · Done Channel Broadcast Cancellation

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/task.sai"
@import "sa_std/globals.sai"
@import "sa_std/ctx.sla"
fn worker(done: Chan<u64>) {
    while !is_done(done) {
        let rc = sa_task_yield();
        if rc != 0 { panic(701); };
    }
    let rc2 = sa_global_u64_set("doneflag", 8, 1);
    if rc2 != 0 { panic(702); };
}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let rc0 = sa_global_u64_set("doneflag", 8, 0);
    let done: Chan<u64> = done_new();
    let h = go worker(done);
    let i: u64 = 0;
    while i < 100 {
        let y = sa_task_yield();
        i = i + 1;
    }
    done_signal(done);
    let st = sa_task_join(h);
    if st != 0 { panic(703); };
    let flag: u64 = 0;
    let rc = sa_global_u64_get("doneflag", 8, &flag);
    println("cancelled = {}", flag);
    done.destroy();
    return 0;
}

Measured output:

cancelled = 1

The sa_std/ctx.sla idiom: Done is a Chan<u64> that is only closed, never sent on; done_signal closing it broadcasts to all workers, and a worker probes non-blockingly with is_done, then exits and sets the flag. The echo server example in the acceptance set is the server form of the same idiom.

16. External Evaluation Settlement (2026-10-30)

This section registers two external evaluations (Mistral, OpenAI, forwarded by the user on 2026-10-30) and the settlement after checking them item by item against our own documents and corpus: only verified items are entered; items that did not hold or that belong to an existing implementation are not registered.

The yield-point set (a shrinkage point; true). Current state: the SLA compiler inserts no yields at all — no loop back-edge yields, no call-site yields; it yields only at blocking runtime calls (already put in writing in TS-13, Section 11). This stance is weaker than the original wording of the Section 7 S2 ruling, and weaker than Go 1.13 (whose function entries have stack checks doubling as preemption points): a loop containing no blocking call can starve a carrier thread forever. Consequence: budget-based yielding v2 rises from a comfortable upgrade item to a must-do item; the user ruled on 2026-10-30: keep the original ordering, budget-based yielding v2 is not moved earlier; the three-machine rework copes by hand-inserting yield, v2 still advances in phase two per the original ordering, and the warning has been issued to each line.

The depth of effect rule R2 (a shrinkage point; true). R2's adopted stance was “write suspends / traps into signatures, statically checked by the compiler”; what was delivered is a shallow syntactic rule: two checkpoints, one is_async boolean, resetting at closure boundaries, reaching neither transitive calls nor direct blocking extern calls. The promise of “eliminating function coloring” is so far redeemed only at the syntactic layer; a transitive coloring appendix awaits a new checker analysis pass, scheduled separately, and this section truthfully registers that gap.

Rejection corpus evidence (supplementary citation). An external evaluation once pointed out that “no rejection corpus evidence was seen” — the checking conclusion is that the corpus is real and the document had not cited it: the corpus of compile-time rejection forms is in the sa_plugin_sla repo's tests/, with 39 files in the test_error_* series + 16 files in diagnostics/ (of which the 9 go_diag_* files are this batch's concurrency-surface diagnostics), judged as rejections by the independent frontend sla check. This page had not cited it before; this section adds the citation. The coverage of competitive forms can still be strengthened, which is follow-up work for the compiler line.

Warnings for the three machines (adopted and issued). Of the external evaluations' warnings for the three-machine rework, four were verified true and have been written into the Ordering Two charters of each line: (1) CPU-dense loops such as TLS handshakes can starve a carrier thread under zero inserted yields, so yield must be hand-inserted or budget-based yielding v2 awaited; (2) under select's declaration-order bias, fan-in collection loops must actively rotate the arm order; (3) globals' single-mutex total-order serialization must not leak into the three machines' hot paths; (4) a long-lived process's entry stack depth must be defined (on the evidence of the three-surface inconsistency in Section 13). The slanginx and db lines started with these four items, and the slaredis line carried them the same way when it started.

17. DEF Compiler Defect Line Closing Record (Batches One to Three, 2026-10-30)

Line opening and stance: the DEF line takes over the base-point defect registrations of Section 14 and the compiler / runtime defects exposed by the Ordering Two three-machine work (the nine surfaces A–I of slaredis's registration in Section 6 of Document 15 were transferred into this line's classification). All readings are four-part: (1) rc=0, (2) the output contains the expected result line, (3) the failure name set is empty (looking only at counts is forbidden), (4) for dual-backend features, both backends pass; negative examples are read with the independent frontend sla check, not the test runner; every fix must carry a minimal reproduction corpus that first fails on an independent pristine baseline tree and passes on both backends after the fix. The evidence is fully recorded in the main-session workspace def12-local/REPORT_NOTES.md (a section per batch, one to three).

Batch one (four surfaces) closed and integrated: DEF-1 — an inline array field of a by-value struct copy moved only one aggregate word in SAB, and a field load did not decay to an address; fixed as an element-by-element recursive copy + array field decay (the corpus baseline SAB failure set was exactly {1111, 1112, 1143, segfault ×2}, and after the fix 7/7 on both backends); the first three surfaces of DEF-2 — SAB's String.as_bytes had no lowering (UnknownRegister 1007), the text backend's len(bare pointer) wrongly emitted a STRING_LEN distortion, and a literal → String parameter segfaulted in SAB, each surface with its own corpus, all passing on both backends after the fix; DEF-KB-1 — a struct handle field's (a Vec/String 8-byte heap handle's) load view was disposed of with a move_, while the verifier's consume of a bare-pointer register is a no-op, so the temporary survived to a control-flow merge point and triggered PhiStateConflict 1015; fixed so a field-view register is disposed of with a real release (corpus 4/4 on both backends, and the Heng kb natural case was unblocked with it, see Section 6 of Document 20); DEF-3 — after a Result/Option enum constructor stored a non-Copy payload, the source binding was not marked moved, and the source was released on the spot, leaving a dangling reference (both backends); fixed by marking moved at the construction point (the corpus baseline had SAB segfault ×4, and after the fix 6/6 on both backends). Suite gate: the fixed tree and the baseline tree, under the same stance, were identical across the 331 indexes one by one (226 OK / FAIL exactly {idx54} / HANG 104 the same set, the failure name set did not grow).

DEF-4 fixed (in the form ruled by Jev): stack_alloc inside a never-returning loop body ratchets and eats the fixed stack iteration by iteration (slaredis registrations C / I, and slanginx's stack ratchet with the same signature). The fix layer was ruled by Jev = host_alloca_rewind 0.50 (sla_hoisting 0.44, hybrid 0.06, confidence 0.25, nearly tied; the host form succeeded on its first try with no principle wall, so no parallel form trials were opened). Implementation, sci 1b5b31e568818814a6e016870d63b8564711b6d4: the LLVM emission shim (src/emit_llvm_llvmc_shim.c) recognizes a loop header label targeted by a back-edge jump; when the header is reached, llvm.stacksave() is stored into a dedicated slot in the entry block, and llvm.stackrestore runs before each back-edge (the clang VLA pattern); it is disabled under wasm_compat. A/B evidence: a distilled probe segfaulted on both backends at baseline and gave rc=0 after the fix (3 million iterations @ ulimit -s 2048); three corpus pieces (an out-parameter cell with 2.5 million iterations / a plain-recv chan loop with 100k / a five-arm select with 20k on a buffered arm) gave 3/3 on both backends after the fix, with the baseline dying on every variant. Coverage is LLVM only: the C backend's sa_salloc is a linear-memory bump allocation (a different surface), the JS backend's linear memory has the same-family ratchet, and Wasm does not support stack_alloc — three residues registered on record, not closed with this commit. Slaredis registration E (pushing into a Vec field inside a loop overflowing the stack) was closed after mapping with three distilled forms: the loop body has no stack_alloc, and 100k pushes on a 256 KiB stack pass on both backends at baseline, its growth attributed to the accompanying chan operations, i.e. DEF-4 itself.

DEF-5 implemented, DEF-2 fully closed (batch two closing): the extraction semantics of a borrowed handle field were ruled by Jev = clone_on_extract 0.86 (extraction is a deep clone and the new binding truly owns it; view_without_drops 0.14), and sla 35a5d1dd87805ee069214b6c5ef2e6ff8317c8e9 set cloneBorrowedHandleFieldValue in both backends' codegen alike. Corpus: baseline on both backends 1015 / signal 6 / 1008, after the fix SAB 3/3; the text surface was 1/3 at the time, the remainder blocked by DEF-6 (see batch three; after the DEF-6 fix the text surface is also 3/3, and this surface is fully closed on both backends). DEF-2's fourth surface (globals string keys silently producing wrong codes on host-direct) gave GLOBALS_OK on all four routes on a new box's sci-built host and did not reproduce, characterized as a stock sa 0.1.8 host artifact — DEF-2 is thus fully closed on all four surfaces. Two items registered in the same batch: the SAB unbuffered five-arm select wedging reproduced with the same signature on the baseline host (previously masked by DEF-4's death at about 643 iterations), assigned to the DEF-R6 runtime waiter-semantics family; and the Heng kb natural case's task-stack demand of (2MiB, 4MiB] did not fall with DEF-4 — its appetite is a single-frame giant (kb_worker's four 64 KiB local arrays + about 264 KiB of slot-literal temporaries), belonging to the DEF-R2 capacity surface, a different combination from DEF-4's signature. Integration (main-session guard push, ls-remote double recheck): six sla cherry-picks (the four commits of the four-surface batch + the DEF-4 corpus 12aebd634a8b4179ca7089e7dcf152027098a60e + DEF-5) with zero conflicts, master 47ec56a → 617c130981d84758cb2d1dc98991c138cbc0693f; one sci commit (1b5b31e5) cherry-picked, main 9c874290 → e7b5ca69b5adba65a4469108534b746b93bd6c22.

Batch three closed and integrated (DEF-6 / DEF-6b / DEF-R1): DEF-6 (sla c1448ca88a759e5c6244e8b344f067e94b2fdecb) — the text backend mistranslated ordinary String rebinding: identifier assignment dispatch took the place-store path even for addressable-only bindings, writing the new handle into the first word of the old String object (a silent wrong code, with the same signature at baseline); the root cause is that addressable only means a borrow / macro argument may take an address on demand, a non-primitive type has no stack-slot materialization, and the value is in a register. The fix makes place-store recognize only stack_alloc_bindings, with addressable-only falling back to release-and-rebind (the general rebinding idiom; SAB needed no change). Corpus of 6 cases: baseline SAB 6/6, text 1/6 (the failure set exactly {straight line, branch merge, sibling, chain, content check}, with Vec rebinding already passing at baseline), and after the fix 6/6 on both backends; a rerun of the DEF-5 corpus rose with it from baseline text 2/3 to 3/3 on both backends. 18. Platform Parity Plan (proposed on 2026-10-30)

Requirement (the user's own order, 2026-10-30 21:05–21:07): every SA build platform must support goroutines, natively or by simulation, and wasm must support them. The semantic surface of parity = spawn / chan / select / join / detach / sleep / mutex; the same piece of SLA code is not rewritten for the concurrency model on any build target — falling short of parity is not a “target-inherent limitation” but a parity gap awaiting completion.

Connection with the correction: the wasm item in Section 4's hard boundaries already records the user's 2026-10-29 correction — the registration nature of phase one's explicit UNSUPPORTED for wasm is a mechanism difference, not a denial in principle (phase one's x86_64 native stack-pointer switching mechanism cannot be used for wasm and must take an independent lowering track). This plan does not overturn the phase-one closing; it formally proposes as a project the independent track that was reserved at registration time: that item's target state advances from “explicitly unsupported” to “simulated support up to standard”.

The two-layer model:

  • Inside an instance: cooperative goroutines. On a single-threaded host (wasm / JS), all goroutines are multiplexed onto one thread with cooperative scheduling, semantically equivalent to GOMAXPROCS=1 on a native platform: blocking operations (chan reads/writes, sleep, host callbacks) yield correctly, and pure CPU loops are not asynchronously preempted. This layer fits the established contract seamlessly — Sections 11 and 16 have settled that “the compiler inserts no yield points, and CPU-dense loops hand-insert sa_task_yield() in the program”; on a single-threaded target this stance rises from a warning to the semantics itself.
  • Between instances: true parallelism (two candidate routes). One is Worker multi-instance (the user's proposal, 2026-10-30 21:14; this language's JS target can use it directly): each Web Worker / Node worker_threads loads an independent instance, scheduling stays cooperative inside an instance and truly parallel across cores; a chan across Workers uses a SharedArrayBuffer ring buffer + Atomics.wait/notify as a blocking transport. The boundary must be stated: in-instance shared state ((*ptr).field, globals) does not cross Workers; only messages cross the boundary, and multi-instance parallelism must not be disguised as shared-memory goroutines; the browser's SharedArrayBuffer requires the page to have cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP response headers), which our own SA HTTP server can emit itself, satisfying the whole stack by itself, while Node worker_threads has no such constraint. The other is the WASM threads proposal (multiple threads inside a single instance). The two routes have been ruled by Jev (see “Advancement and acceptance” at the end of this section): the parallel layer is deferred in phase one and semantic parity is delivered first; of the two routes, Worker multi-instance is retained as phase two's preferred candidate (this tree's JS emitter's net bridge already has working evidence of a worker + SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics.wait to draw on), and WASM threads is not the current main line.

Reference evidence: Go's official wasm port is a ready-made precedent — both GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm (Go 1.11+) and GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm (Go 1.21+) package the full runtime (including the scheduler and GC) into a wasm module, and goroutines / channels / select all work normally; its limitations are likewise single-threaded, cooperative scheduling, no asynchronous preemption, and no multi-core acceleration — that is, “concurrency complete, parallelism absent”, exactly isomorphic to this plan's in-instance layer delimitation. The platform parity mapping line has been executed by the user-specified method; however, this machine has no Go toolchain and could not compile locally, so this item's conclusion is source-level evidence (a conclusion reached by reading Go's official runtime source directly), not masquerading as a locally compiled and run re-verification, and this stance is noted expressly.

Current state of each target (mapping finalized, 2026-10-30):

  • native (LLVM): supported, x86_64 Linux only — runtime phase one + the SLA syntax surface + DEF-4 stack rewinding + DEF-R1 sa_task_detach, empirically proven in production form by slanginx / slaredis / db (see Sections 10, 14, and 17 of this page and Document 15). The scope is tightened from the earlier general stance: context switching for aarch64 / Windows / macOS is not implemented and is likewise ERR_UNSUPPORTED on those hosts; their parity belongs to this plan (the aarch64 context assembly delimitation has been listed as a leading small item).
  • wasm: the finalized mapping is still explicitly UNSUPPORTED; DEF-4's host rewinding is disabled under wasm_compat, linear-memory allocation is an independent surface different from native, and the stackful mechanism is not portable — per the ruling at the end of this section it takes the CPS / state-machine simulation track, which is this plan's main target.
  • JS emission: not implemented — the sa_task semantic surface has zero bindings in the JS emitter; this current-state wording is frozen from this section on as “not implemented” and is no longer phrased as “being mapped”.
  • C emission: not implemented, with a stdlink shortcut — the C target can draw on a host-side implementation through stdlink's ready-made channel, so the cost of completing parity is lower than implementing from zero; its acceptance must be read separately on the two routes C→native and C→wasm (the latter ultimately still lands on the wasm track). The C / JS backend linear-memory ratchet residues recorded for DEF-4 in Section 17 are coordinated by this plan from this section on (that item in the DEF remaining sequence takes this plan as its home).

Structural conclusion (mapping finalized): the SLA frontend's lowering is target-independent — the same frontend lowering product can feed any target backend; whether there is parity is purely a question of the per-target runtime, i.e. of the presence of a scheduler, context switching, and chan / select in each target's runtime, unrelated to the frontend. The plan's implementation form is therefore fixed as: complete each target's runtime, with no frontend fork; the three simulation targets ruled on below sharing one state-machine transformation is the direct corollary of this conclusion.

Advancement and acceptance (mapping and ruling complete, 2026-10-30): the mapping product PARITY.md has been finalized (a four-target × semantic-surface matrix, candidate mechanisms with cost scores, and an acceptance matrix), stored in the main-session workspace goroutine-parity-local/. The route fork was sent to Jev for a double ruling (2026-10-30, executed by the main session, adopted by default, overturnable by the user; the ruling is at jev-designs/goroutine_parity_ruling.json): the main mechanism = CPS / state-machine shared lowering 0.95 (confidence 0.93; not selected: the dual-track CPS+JSPI 0.04, Asyncify first 0.01, JSPI first 0.00) — the wasm / JS / C targets share one compiler-level state-machine transformation and each carries only a small driver layer; it is the only route that can cover all hosts (including wasm32-wasi and arbitrary WASI embedders); JSPI and Asyncify are out, both because their scheduling authority sits in a host outside the module and they cannot cover general WASI embedders. The parallel layer = deferred in phase one 0.97 (confidence 0.96; not selected: Worker multi-instance first 0.02, WASM threads 0.01) — phase one delivers only semantic parity, on the same scale as Go's official wasm; its known cost (if phase two chooses the in-instance shared-memory route, it may have to change phase one's surface contract retroactively) is expressly recorded in the ruling as an informed deferral, and Worker multi-instance is retained as phase two's preferred candidate. Subsequent sequence: the leading fork-independent small items first (freezing the JS / C current-state wording as “not implemented” — done in this section; mapping the C1 stdlink shortcut; delimiting the aarch64 context assembly) → a single-target CPS prototype (taking 6 existing goroutine corpus pieces as a subset, accepted by four-part reading) → then generalizing to the other targets. Implementation is scheduled after the DEF main line and coordinated with the std improvement batch; the CXU frontend (in SA wasm form) is a direct beneficiary. The development goal has been proposed as the Goals goal “SA all-platform goroutine parity” (its charter is in the main-session workspace goals/sa-goroutine/GOAL.md); this section records only the plan stance, and the details follow that charter and PARITY.md. 22. STRIDE-1 / DEF-8 Contract and DEF-11 Registration (2026-10-31)

Contract (finalized; the same text is in the helper file's header comment): a Vec's element slot is always word-sized — the stride = max(元素 ABI 尺寸, 8) bytes; this is the common internal design of the whole std macro surface and both backends and is not to be changed. The raw data pointer given by VEC_AS_PTR / VEC_AS_SLICE is a slot-stride layout, not a C-style packed array (for Vec<u8> [104, 105], raw byte 1 is padding and the second element is at byte 8); handing the raw pointer directly to an extern that reads it as packed is a usage error. When a packed byte mirror is needed, use sa_vec_export_packed_{u8,u16,i32,f64} from sa_std/vec_packed.sla (a pure SLA implementation, no new extern): it packs tightly by element ABI size, little-endian, writes into the caller's buffer, and returns (status, bytes) — status 0 = the mirror has been written and bytes is the byte count; status 1 = the buffer capacity is insufficient, dst is not written by a single word, and bytes = the required capacity (so the caller can grow and retry); it never silently truncates; an empty Vec returns (0, 0). The implementation form was ruled by Jev = packed_export_helper 0.98; type coverage was ruled in a second round as expand-on-demand (delimit_on_demand 0.54), and the four types are this batch's closing state.

DEF-11 registration (Vec<f64> storage semantics, an independent batch): sa_vec_push's value parameter is a u64, and on push an f64 is numerically converted rather than stored by bit pattern (sla repo demos/basic/POTENTIAL_ISSUES.md #24, confirmed 2026-10-10); the two backends' symptoms diverge (under SAB, after push(1.5) the slot's byte7 = 0 and the read-back ≠ 1.5; under the text backend byte7 = 0x3F and the read-back still ≠ 1.5), and the SLA layer has no bitcast surface. So DEF-8's f64 export can currently pin only the contract level (status and byte count) and the 0.0 all-zero mirror; byte-level correctness follows DEF-11. Jev has ruled separate_defect_line 0.98: DEF-11 fixes Vec<f64>'s by-bit-pattern storage semantics as its own batch, and when it lands, the vec_packed f64 corpus gains byte-level assertion lines (1.5 → 00 00 00 00 00 00 F8 3F).

23. DEF-12 Registration and Fix Delivery; Review (b) Residual Registration (2026-10-31)

DEF-12 filed: the form in which the Heng validate_kb and json natural cases were stuck by the checker's BorrowConflict was triaged and characterized as the checker implementation layer being over-conservative, not a view-types second-order design problem: within one call, one argument is a borrow of some place and another argument is a by-value read of a Copy-type place (evaluation copies it, with no aliasing risk), and the old accounting rejected all of these uniformly as a borrowed-vs-plain conflict. The fix surface = checkCallArgPlaceOverlaps (type_checker.zig). The danger pin was pinned first: the combination of a borrow + a whole-Vec-field move must keep being rejected.

The fix has been delivered (staging; integration follows the remote head): commit 21eea153 (branch def12-fix, base point fc46620a, 7 files +252/−4: the src/type_checker.zig fix + 6 corpus pieces). Mechanism: a plain-side argument first passes the new criterion plainArgIsCopyRead — a by-value read of a Copy-type place does not enter the borrowed-vs-plain judgment; a true move of a non-Copy stays rejected; type retrieval goes through the new side-effect-free placeExprType (mirroring the field/index/deref type rules, returning null when it cannot be determined, and treating that as no exemption); the signature path and the two macro paths share the same classification. The read-only exemption route was not taken. Evidence: the three distilled reproduction forms (parameter forwarding, an explicit &doc, and the same form via an extern) went from RC 1 on the pristine baseline plugin to RC 0 after the fix, with the legal controls at RC 0 on both trees; the danger pin preserved the same diagnostic at RC=1 on both trees; the natural cases validate_kb.sla and json.sla both went from sla check RC 1 → 0 (all five same-pattern call sites accounted for one by one, with no remaining diagnostics); the 332 batch gate gave 329/3 on both trees, with the failure set identical index by index and name by name, {55, 106, 107}. Unproven surfaces, truthfully: the macro-path combination (a borrow slot + a Copy read at the same point) was not given its own corpus and is covered by the shared function-body structure; placeExprType returns null for Rc/Arc/Box dereferences and keeps the baseline rejection, an intentionally conservative boundary. At the time this section was written, that commit's serial integration was in progress, and the landing head follows the remote.

Review (b) residual registration (stock; the proposal awaits a ruling): the false UseAfterMove of a nested call outer(inner(v)) still has a residual surface after the in-batch fix — a non-chan fall-through path double-checks a nested call's by-value arguments. The probes are in integ-wave/work/probes_b/: P2 destroy(b_pass(s)) and P3 len(b_mkvec(s)) show the same diagnostic on both trees, the integration tree and the pristine baseline fc46620a, characterized as a stock tail item, not introduced by the integration wave; P1/P4's true chan shapes pass at both the checker layer and SAB (the in-batch fix holds for chan shapes); P4 additionally shows a stock MemoryLeak signature on the text backend (the method-temporary layer, a different layer from the checker residue), also on record. The candidate fix form (wrapping the probe with a snapshot / restore, mirroring the overloading probe mechanism) is not within review (a)'s same-mechanism authorization and was not touched this round; the failing corpus is not put into tests/, to avoid polluting the 332 name set, pending a main-session ruling to propose it as a project.

24. DEF-R8 Ruling and DEF-R8-FIX Registration (2026-10-31)

Ruling: a true leak, with two root causes. Under a slanginx-shaped load, RSS grows linearly with requests (about 6.4–6.5 KB/req, not decaying); LD_PRELOAD allocation accounting closed it byte by byte, characterizing it as a true leak in our code, not allocator retention (the provisional classification of the time in Section 19 is corrected here):

  • Root cause one (sci): the native LLVM backend never releases SA-level allocations — emit_llvm_llvmc.zig hard-codes the .ty of .release as .void, making the shim's free path unreachable; the interpreter and the emit_c / emit_js surfaces all truly release.
  • Root cause two (sla): releases are mis-marked at value-transfer points — for example, a Box::new argument is still emitReleased after being stored into a cell.

Evidence magnitude: distilled probe h4 is 128 B/cycle (exactly 4 named blocks), A2 is 64.0 B/cycle, C is about 31.5 B/cycle, with the accounting fully closed; the slanginx load-test form is about 6.4–6.5 KB/req. The fix form was ruled by Jev = option_a_joint_batch 1.0 (both root causes fixed in the same batch).

DEF-R8-FIX in-progress registration: the fix line has opened (site def-r8fix-local): on the sci side, F1 restores the LLVM backend's free; on the sla side, a full audit of value-transfer points (call arguments, Vec/container pushes, struct field materialization, tuple returns, spawn arguments, chan sends, closure captures — point-by-point probe → fix → corpus), with interpreter exposure-surface tests attached; the acceptance gate = the h4/A2/C slopes going to zero, an MALLOC_PERTURB_ rerun, zero drift in the 332 and sa-std-unit name sets, and a slanginx endurance slope of ≈0 over ≥150k requests. A stop-loss line is on record: if the audit finds a systemic emission-rule gap, the line stops and is repackaged and sent to Jev.

slaredis's payload-proportional RSS defect merged under this umbrella: empirically proven by the slaredis optimization line — each SET's RSS growth is about ×57 of the payload (poll build) / ×91 (goroutine build), linear and never reclaimed, reproducing equally with AOF off (starting at 11.5 MB → 524 MB after a 4 MiB SET → 1.09 GB after one clean GET); a pure Vec micro-probe is healthy and the journal has been excluded. The availability consequence in the same scenario: a 4 MiB reply meeting a client disconnect mid-way gets the process OOM-killed (SIGKILL 137) — the R7 disconnect-survival case passes at a 64 KiB reply and is blocked by this defect at 4 MiB, and the two stances are registered separately. That form and this section's ruling corroborate each other as the same family; root cause and fix belong to DEF-R8 / DEF-R8-FIX, with no separate number.

25. New Defect Registrations (2026-10-31, three items)

Registration one: the BorrowConflict same-container double shared-borrow corner (checker). Two elements of the same container appearing together in one call as shared borrows — such as bytes_eq(&args[k], &args[j]) — are rejected with BorrowConflict (args[_] / args[_] overlapping). Shared + shared borrows never conflict semantically, so this is a precision defect in the checker's place accounting, of the same family as the first-order view-types duck double-borrow corner note, but of a different shape from DEF-12's Copy-read form, and registered separately. There are 4 samples (the HSET / SADD / ZADD deduplication scans in the slaredis repo's commands.sla and the member comparison in zrows_before; the source evidence is in §1 of slaredis-opt-local/REPORT.md); the slaredis side has worked around it with the semantically equivalent reshape bytes_eq_elems (a single container borrow + index reads), merged into its build fix commit, and the checker body's fix awaits DEF triage.

Registration two: the host verifier MemoryLeak 1012 module-context trap (verifier). The helper function @sla__aof_config_from_env, which returns an (i32, AofConfig) tuple, is judged MemoryLeak 1012 in a full-module build (a register still Active at the final return), while the character-for-character identical function compiles and passes standalone, and the two lowering products are character-for-character identical on that function — the triggering condition is at module scale / in context. The evidence pair is preserved at the slaredis site: work/main_failing_1012.sa (failing) against work/repro2_aofcfg.sa (passing). This line did not dig deeper, per its stop-loss line; the application side reshaped to a struct return (AofConfigResult) and the full build passed. The verifier body's characterization and fix await filing triage.

Registration three: sa_http_server_accept_v2's timeout unification (sci runtime). Location src/runtime/sa_http_server.zig:2169: the same timeout serves both as the readiness poll slice and as the total budget for parsing a fresh connection's head (acceptBounded passes the remaining budget to both the poll and acceptFresh's parse_timeout). Consequence: under load, a scheduling delay over 1 ms makes parsing fail and the connection is closed (the client sees an Empty reply). A same-window ladder test (load about 19): slices of 1 / 50 / 250 ms → 33 / 48 / 50 successes out of 50 sequential connections. A comparison precedent: the connection-pool path already has an independent probe_parse_timeout_ms=50, i.e. there is an existing example of the parse budget decoupled from the poll. The application layer's only knob is the slice itself, which conflicts directly with slanginx c1's slice tax, and there is no application-layer solution; the fix direction = decoupling the two budgets, assigned to an sci fix batch.
